Hello and welcome to Venkatesh Bhat’s Idhayam Thotta Samayal. Today I’m happy to meet you with another fantastic recipe. Many of you have been asking for various recipes and I’ve been filtering the most-requested ones. On that note, one of the most requested recipe was Vada curry. It is very famous and there is no competition for Saidapet Vada curry. It has retained its fame through many generations and years as a colloquial local dish. Vada Curry’s close companion/best friend is Set Dosa! It is more of a friend than Idly to Vada curry! So, let me tell you how to prepare Set Dosa and Vada curry. I’ve mentioned Teynampet’s Durga hotel in previous videos. Nagraj master’s Vada curry had an intense rivalry with Vellachami’s Set dosa. (The grinding master) It was such a deadly combo. So, I’m going to teach you that deadly combination today. I’m going to demonstrate Vada curry as per how I learnt in the hotel. There are no tomatoes or coconut milk in this recipe. But many hotels utilize tomato to make it. However, since I learnt it this way in our hotel, I’m going to demonstrate the same. Think of this as a method that skips tomato. I have a pan here, it is heated. To the pan, without adding oil, add 6-8 cloves. 4-5 pieces of cinnamon. 6-8 Elaichis. 4 slit green chillies. Dry roast them. Add chopped garlic. It is better to add it in excess because it’s flavour is very important. Garlic, Khus Khus/Poppy seeds and Saunf are very important for the end product’s flavour. Next is ginger. Suppose you have added 100g of garlic, add 60g of ginger. It should be lesser in comparison. So, to recap, ginger, garlic, green chilli, Elaichi, Cinnamon and cloves have been added so far. Dry roast them. Add 2 tsp of Saunf. A handful of Roasted grams. 1 tbsp of Khus Khus. 8 round red chillies. Add all of these and roast them further. This will bring out the flavour and aroma of the ingredients. You will get the smell of tempting roadside food stalls! After it is roasted well, add some coriander leaves and some pudina. Roast further. After the Khus Khus and roasted gram roast/pop, add ½ coconut (grated) Roast briefly like so. Turn off the gas after adding coconut. The heat of the pan is enough to roast the coconut. The flavours of all the ingredients form an intense combo! After it cools down to room temperature, we have to grind it to a fine paste. Now we have prepared the base masala for the vada curry gravy, all that’s left is to grind it. Now to prepare the vada, we have to soak chana dal (300g), 6-7 round red chillies and a spoon of Saunf for 3 hours. This has to be ground to a coarse paste after soaking (3 hours) and straining the water from it. It shouldn’t be too fine, and should be coarse like masala vada consistency. Now both the soaked and strained Vada mixture and masala mixture have gone for grinding. Now, let’s look at the method of preparing Set Dosa batter. For that, we need 1kg of dosa rice, 150g Urad dal, 150g of Aval/Poha. The Aval has to be soaked in buttermilk (add 2 tumblers of water to 100g of curd and beat) for 15 minutes. The aval will absorb the buttermilk. So, one hand, you will be soaking 1kg of dosa rice, 150g Urad dal and 25-30g (1 ½ tsp) Methi/Fenugreek seeds. And on the other hand, you will be soaking Aval in buttermilk. The first mixture of dosa rice, urad and fenugreek should be soaked for 3-4 hours. After soaking, strain the water and grind to a fine paste. As it grinds, strain the excess buttermilk from the Aval and add the Aval to the grinder and grind further. It will take around 30 mins for it to finish grinding in a grinder. After grinding, add required salt, beat it well and let it ferment overnight. (8 hours) After 8 hours, the batter will have expanded in volume. After obtaining this, I’ll tell you the further steps to prepare set dosa. Now, the mixture for the Vada has been ground to a coarse paste. Transfer to a bigger bowl. Add some Hing powder and salt and mix well. Some people prefer to add chilli powder, onion, turmeric powder etc. Nothing wrong in following a different method. But this is the method I learnt in our hotel. Some people also boil small balls of this in an idly steamer. That is also one type of vada curry. But vada fried in oil has the better taste. That is why I will be demonstrating the same. Look at how it is ground, there isn’t a trace of the red chilli. Here, I have heated up some oil. When adding this to the oil, it always dissociates. So generally, we don’t add it as pre-mould shape. So just add it to the oil like so. There is no shape required for it. After removing it, we are anyway going to crush it and add to the curry. So, it doesn’t make much of a difference. It shouldn’t turn out too crispy like masala vada. Only when it ¾ fried, it is able to absorb the gravy. If it over-fried, then it won’t absorb the gravy. So, after adding, remove it around the 2-minute mark when it starts changing colour. Observe, just fry the random shapes like so. When it turns brown, remove it and strain the oil. That’s it, this is the right colour. When we add this to the Vada Curry gravy, we are going to cook it further for about 2 minutes. That time it will cook well. The benefit of adding the pieces randomly without a shape is that, the smaller pieces will be more crunchy And the bigger pieces will be soft and will give a wonderful texture to the Vada curry. If you fry this even more and make it crispy, it is a fantastic coffee time snack or starter. It is a wonderful vada with a fantastic combination of flavours. Next to Vani mahal, T-nagar, around 25 years ago, there was a place that used to serve Sundal, Vada, Potato Bonda, Pudina chutney etc. When I returned from school, I’d have a plate of Sundal Vada before taking the bus. If my parents knew, then they would give me an earful since it was a roadside place! But the taste of the Masala vada there is unparalleled. First, they add Sundal, crush vada on top and then, a ladle of pudina chutney. It was wonderful! So just like that, this can be eaten as a fantastic starter! Now the Vada for Vada curry is ready. Let’s prepare the curry. The masala paste for the gravy has been kept ready and the Vada is ready over there as well. Now, let’s prepare the gravy. Firstly, add 5 tbsp of oil. The quantity I will be preparing can be accommodated in this bowl. I do not know how many people it will be sufficient for in different households. But as per my household, it can serve around 6-7 people. So, I’ve taken 5 tbsp of oil. To it, add 2 pieces of cinnamon and 2 cloves. (It is already present in the paste, but we’re adding it anyway for the taste) 4 elaichis. Then, 1 tsp of Saunf. 4 round red chillies. A handful of curry leaves. When it fries, add 2 sliced medium size onions. Mix and fry well. The onion has to roast well. If you want the onion to turn golden brown quickly, add some salt, it will change colour quicker. I’m not going to add ginger garlic paste to this. But if you wish to add it for its flavour, You may do so at this stage and fry till the onion turns golden brown and the paste is cooked. I’m not going to be adding since the masala paste already has ginger and garlic. The onion has to cook succulently and turn juicy. It has cooked and roasted well. At this stage, add the pre-prepared masala paste. Cook the paste well with the onion and the oil. The aroma will be very strong because of the ingredients it contains! When it mixes with the onion, pour 4-5 tumblers of water Mix the paste well in the water. If you wish to add tomato, do so after you finish cooking onion and ginger garlic paste previously. But Nagaraj master didn’t add tomato and since I’m demonstrating the same recipe, I won’t be adding it as well. You will definitely ask in the comments if tomatoes can be added. So, add it at the aforementioned period of time. After adding water, we have to bring it to a boil. Before that, add 1 tsp of turmeric powder. 1 ½ tsp of Kashmiri chilli powder (for its colour) So, I’ve added 1 tsp of turmeric powder and 1 ½ tsp of Kashmiri chilli powder. Observe, the gravy is starting to boil. It has a vibrant colour! Add required salt. Boil it till the raw smell goes away. It will turn thick quickly since it contains Khus Khus and coconut. That is why I’ve added 5 tumblers of water. So, boil it using little extra water so that it gets the cooked aroma. I have added only 2 onions but you may add up to 4 onions if you prefer. Beautiful! It has boiled well. At this stage, Add the fried vadas. Crumble them like so. Since we added chana dal, it will turn thick very quickly. The vada will absorb the water very quickly And so, 30 minutes after you turn off the gas, it will have turned thick. In that case, pour a little hot water and dilute it, then serve. That problem will not arise if you add tomato. It will give both sourness and moisture content to the gravy. But I will not be using it. Super! Fantastic roadside Saidapet Vada curry. Have it with set dosa! Make sure the gravy is slightly watery, pour it on a set dosa and place another dosa on top. It will be ultimate and you can have it for breakfast lunch or dinner! Vada curry is ready! Before plating it, add a lavish sprinkle of coriander and a fist of curry leaves. Saidapet Vada curry, ready! Here, the Dosa batter is ready, consisting of Aval, Urad, Dosa rice and fenugreek seeds. It will be somewhat thick. They say that set dosa turns out good no matter what consistency it turns out to be. What differentiates it from a normal batter is the fact that it has Aval and less urad. I'm taking some batter from this. You can make the dosa with this batter itself, it will be good. However, it will be soft like an ordinary dosa, like how they make in Bangalore. To the batter, add 1 tsp of sugar. Required salt. ½ tsp of turmeric powder. Little more than ½ a tsp of cooking soda/Appam soda. There is enough batter for 15 no. set dosa. Here I have some water. Adjust the measurement as per the consistency. It should have a flowing consistency i.e. when you pour it on the tawa, it should spread out on its own. So add water accordingly. That is why the batter should be slightly watery. As soon as you add the cooking soda, it will puff up due to air coagulation. Stir to mix the ingredients well. It should be slightly thicker than Wheat dosa batter. The batter is ready. The dosa tawa has heated. Take a ladle of batter and pour it. Observe, it is spreading out on its own. Don’t do anything else, just close it with a lid. A good set dosa is said to be obtained when it has numerous holes on the surface! This is due to air coagulation which leads to bubbling. When such holes appear, the set dosa is ready. Let it cook for 2-3 mins under a closed lid on slow flame. After that, open the lid, smear some oil and remove it. Observe, many holes have formed. At this stage, just sprinkle some oil and plate it. Place a banana leaf on it. Pour the batter for another dosa. It should always be in a pair. Only then is it a ‘set’. So always serve as a pair. When you cook it on slow flame for 5 minutes, it will form holes on its own. If it hasn’t formed, it implies that the cooking soda you’ve added is less in quantity. If that is the case, then there will be lesser holes and it won’t be as soft. If you prefer to skip soda, you may avoid it. The aval will provide the softness. But it will take time to form holes. So, what you can do, is to add more Aval. It will compensate by giving it more softness. The Dosa will be soft, however to get numerous holes and a fluffy texture, cooking soda is needed. So you can even do it by adding very little cooking soda. Sprinkle some oil on top and flip it over to cook the other side as well. Doing this will give some colour to the top side as well. That is how you should cook set dosa. In Karnataka, grated carrot, coriander, cashew nuts are added on top and cooked on both sides. Turmeric powder is skipped in that method, it remains white. In Tamil Nadu, the set dosas are yellow in colour but nothing else is added on top. So, cook on both sides, it will be like a soft flower! That’s it! Look at how it is, it is so fluffy and light. Take some Vada curry in a bowl. This is actually a substitute for non-veg food. It is an authentic non-veg masala containing Khus Khus, Saunf, Cinnamon, Elaichi, Cloves, ginger, garlic etc. like for Mutton Kozhambu. It is ready to serve! Fantastic Vada curry with set dosa, just for you in Venkatesh Bhat’s Idhayam Thotta Samayal! My style, Vada curry, make it and enjoy!

Hello and welcome to Venkatesh Bhat’s ‘Idhayam Thotta Samayal’. Today we will be looking at a most requested recipe, Medu Vada. The reason I named it as ‘Mallipoo (Jasmine flower) Medu Vada’ is for its softness. Nothing special, it is the same authentic Medu Vada, you would’ve surely seen it before but I’ll show you the minor nuances involved. The most important thing to make a good Medu Vada is Urad dal. It should be of very high quality. You will get the best result if you grind well-soaked Urad dal in a grinder. But today I will be grinding it in a mixer. There might be some shortcomings such as Vada getting hard, if the Urad dal is not properly soaked, or the quality of the Urad dal is not superior. But let’s see how we can achieve the best result making use of what we have. Most of the people will be preparing this in a mixer, so I will be using a mixer as well. But preparing it in a grinder will always yield the best possible result. But today I will show how to prepare Urad  dal Vada in a mixer. I have soaked Urad  dal(150g) in water for 1 hour at room temperature. I have soaked this only after washing it for 5 times because the outer part of the Urad will have white residue. So you have to clean all that off thoroughly which is why I washed for 5 times. After doing so, I’ve soaked it for 1 hour. Once it is soaked for 1 hour outside, refrigerate the same in a fridge, for another hour. This is because, since we’re grinding it in a mixer, it is essential to keep it refrigerated. The mixer will have a very high-speed motor which generates heat. However, in case of a grinder, it is a slow process. That is why, if you’re grinding it using a stone grinder, then you may skip the refrigeration phase of the soaked Urad. Now I’m going to add this Soaked Urad to the mixer without the residual water. I’m just going to add the Urad and grind it. When grinding, I’m going to add water in around 3 intervals in between. So, add the Urad, let’s see the grinding process. After grinding it for 15 seconds, you will observe that it will have hardened. So just loosen it by giving a quick and firm stir with a spoon. Then add 2tbsp of water to the mixer and resume the grinding. I have ground this for another 15 seconds, there might be some Urad that haven’t been ground properly So, mix again and toss. After mixing, again add 2tbsp of water and grind it. Now, for the third time, add 2tbsp of water, mix it well so that the bottom part may come up and grind well, and start grinding. After adding water 3 times and turning it to a fine paste, transfer it to a bowl. See how soft and puffy it is. Transfer it to a bowl like so. I’m repeating it again, doing it in a mixer involves more difficulty. But grinding it in a grinder will make it come out fantastic! It will have an unreal softness and puffiness. This will make the Vada even softer. So, when doing it in a grinder, Soak the Urad for 1 hour. The process of grinding by adding water 3 times in between, remains the same. The Vada will come out very well. Now our ground Urad paste is ready. I have transferred the paste to a round bowl so that it is easy and convenient to drop the Vadas into the oil like this. This is a useful technique. It is easier to scoop out the paste from a round bowl such as this. So that is the reason I’ve transferred it to this bowl. Now for 150g of Urad that we’ve used to make a paste, add ½ tsp of Asafoetida/Hing. Then add little more than ½ tsp of salt. After adding these, I have some ginger and green chillis here. Chop the required quantity of ginger into fine, thin pieces. I like the flavour of ginger which is why I’m going to use it a little more. If you don’t like it, then you may reduce the quantity. Ginger, Green Chilli, Salt, and Hing are the main essential ingredients for Medu Vada. Any additional ingredients are all modifications to the Vada. Some people add Onion, Curry leaves, Jeera, Red Chilli, Rice powder, cooking soda etc. However, the 4 ingredients I have mentioned, are the only ones required for an authentic Medu Vada. (Chop the green chillies) Anything additionally added like Red Chilli, Jeera, Coconut, Curry leaves are all appropriate ingredients for Mysore Bonda. So, the ingredients used, is the differentiator between Medu Vada and Mysore Bonda. So, after adding Green Chilli, Ginger, Hing, and Salt, Mix well like so. Beat it this way so as to achieve air coagulation and obtain a fluffy batter. Keep in mind that when making Medu Vada, don’t refrigerate the batter or leave it out in the open for more than 30 minutes. If the batter has been left for more than 30min-1 hour, then the Vada will absorb oil excessively while frying and won’t turn out right. These are small techniques. It is always advisable to fry the Vadas as soon as the batter is ready. After beating it like so, wash your hands. Add the batter in the shape of a Vada (with a hole in the middle). After adding the Vada and flipping it for a while, let it fry for 5-6 minutes. We are making a hole in the middle of the Vada so that the oil flows up from the bottom and roasts the side of the Vada. In Bonda, there is no hole in the middle since we want the inside of it to be semi cooked. However, the presence of a hole in Vada, will roast the side of the Vada so that it will be evenly cooked inside. So, fry it on a high flame till it turns golden brown. Try to use a premium quality of Urad so that the Vada will turn out better. Most importantly, I demonstrated today’s recipe in a mixer to show it to you in a quick and easy way, which is why I refrigerated it after soaking it. But if you use a grinder, it will turn out fantastic. My brother, Divakar, is a Vada specialist. So, he had a hotel called ‘City Café’. It was situated in front of a general hospital which was next to a railway station. The Vadas there were fantastic! There was a master for Vadas as well, Mr. Bhaskar. The Vada was so light, one would assume it was floating in the air. The reason for that is because of the quality of Urad they sourced. So, if you use good quality of Urad, you will get a fantastic result. This same recipe of Vada is used in Vada Sambar. Adding curd to the same, will make it Dahi Vada. (Before adding the Vada to the curd, you must soak it in hot water and drain the water from it) Now, it has attained a beautiful golden brown colour. You may now remove it from the oil. After the oil has drained/dripped down from the Vada, transfer it to a bowl. See how it is, it’s as if it will fly away if I blow air on it! So lightweight and beautifully cooked! It has a beautiful golden brown colour. It is crispy on the outside and hollow on the inside. Crispy Medu Vada! We’ve seen how to prepare it at home. Prepare it yourself and enjoy with your family. Do well, All the best!

Hello and welcome to Venkatesh Bhat’s Idhayam Thotta Samayal presented by Idhayam. I will be using Idhayam Sesame oil and Idhayam Groundnut oil to prepare a wide variety of dishes. Today let’s look at the process of preparing an all-time favourite rice item, Tomato rice. The tomato rice I’m going to be preparing today will contain onion,tomato and garlic. If you want to skip those two ingredients, you may do so. Just follow the rest of the process/ingredients Properly, and you will get a tomato rice with no onion and garlic. But onion and garlic, mixed with curry leaves, give a fantastic flavour to the rice if added. It is best to prepare this using groundnut oil because its flavour will go well with this rice. Be it any variety of rice, use groundnut oil in its preparation. (Except coconut rice (coconut oil) and puliyogare (sesame oil)) Let’s look at how to prepare tomato rice. Firstly, I have a kadai here. I’m going to prepare the masala and mix the rice in this itself. So here, I have boiled rice i.e. raw rice cooked 75% in excess boiling water and then strained. So, because of that the rice is puffy and not mushy. Keep this rice ready. Let me tell you what to do next. Light the stove. I’ve added 3 tbsp of Mantra Groundnut oil. Many of you have asked me to mention the measurements in terms of cups and teaspoons Instead of grams etc. Let me tell you one thing, I only have experience in approximating quantities using my sight or by hand. I do not know to tell quantities exactly in terms of grams or spoons. So, there may be some difference between what I tell and what I add. So, kindly pay visual attention to the quantities I add. It might be a bit less or more, But with practice, you’ll get the hang of it. So first, we’re going to prepare a masala for the tomato rice. To the heated oil, Add 1 tsp of mustard. 4 round red chillies. Let the mustard crackle/pop. ½ tsp of Jeera. 1 tsp of Urad dal. 1 tsp of Chana dal. 3 tsp of cashew nuts. Add all these and cook until they turn golden brown. Add some curry leaves as well. The flavours of all these ingredients have started to come out. At this stage, Add 1 ½ chopped onions. (medium size) The quantity of tomatoes we will be going to add, should be double the quantity of onions. For people who wish to skip onion and garlic, you may add tomato at this stage instead of onion. I have finely chopped tomatoes here. Some people use tomato puree instead. Even that will turn out good. So, after adding the onion, I have some finely chopped garlic here. Add 2 tsp of finely chopped garlic. The onion gives a certain sweetness to the dish as it turns golden brown due to caramelization. That sweetness is very important for the dish, that is why I’ve used onion in this dish. People who wish to skip onion and garlic, may do so. If you skip them, it will stay fresh till 3pm if you pack it. (assuming you prepared it in the morning) However, if you use onion and garlic, then make sure to consume it between 12-1 (assuming you prepared it at 8-8:30 a.m.) Because after that, the onion will give out water content and it will start giving off a smell. Now the onion has attained a beautiful golden-brown colour. At this stage, Add the 3 chopped tomatoes. I have used ripe red tomatoes for its bright colour. Mash and cook it. At this stage, add ½ tsp of turmeric powder. I have Kashmiri Chilli powder here for its redness. Add 1 tsp of it. Mix well. The raw smell will go away in about 20 seconds, at that stage, Pour 250ml of water and mix well. Pour 250ml of water and mix well. Now let it boil for 8-10 minutes so that the tomato’s rawness goes away and the masala gives flavour to all ingredients. While it is cooking, slit 1 green chilli into 2, add it and let it continue boiling. Many of you have expressed concern for my health, for example on the Pongal video, by saying that you’ve noticed that I have been breathing heavily or that I have difficulty in breathing. The thing is, firstly, If I start a shoot in the morning, it ends only at night after completing about 10 dishes. This is because it is not feasible for the team to come daily. So, I shoot 10 videos in a day, and then release each of them over the course of a month. Since the shoot starts in the morning and ends at night, I’m required to continuously talk throughout it. So naturally, towards the end, my voice and breathing will get heavy. And since I’m a little fat and age is catching up to me, such things are expected. But by god’s grace and your prayers, I’m hale and healthy. So, thank you for your concern. Observe, the tomatoes have cooked fully in the water that we’ve added. It has to be cooked mushily. At this stage, add the required salt for tomato rice. Since I didn’t add salt to the rice, this salt is for the whole dish, including the rice. Add ½ tsp of Hing/Asafoetida. Since I used local tomatoes, it will have natural sourness. There is another variety called Bengaluru tomato which many people are opting for these days. But the thing about Bengaluru tomato is that it isn’t as sour as local tomatoes. So, if you use Bengaluru tomato, then squeeze 20g of tamarind in water, and add the water at this stage. It will give the required sourness. If you use regular local tomatoes, then it is not required. Observe, the addition of salt and Hing has given it a glaze. As soon as the mixture came in contact With the sodium, it started giving out its natural colours. It is almost done, at this stage, add a lavish sprinkle of coriander. Now time for my favourite ingredient, add 1 tbsp of ghee. Look at its shine! Add another tablespoon so that the shine remains even after mixing the rice. So, in total, add 2 tbsp of ghee and lower the flame. Now the masala for the tomato rice is ready. Many people add garam masala at this stage but I do not recommend it. It is an ingredient used mainly for biriyani and pulao. In this, there is tomato’s flavour, green chilli and chilli powder for spiciness, and the light taste of Hing Then there are Urad dal and cashew nut which you can chew. Then finally, the flavour of garlic and The sweetness of onion. This is all that required for the dish. It has cooked beautifully. At this stage, add the boiled rice and mix it. Look at the redness! It’s like a red sparkler that burns bright during Diwali! The colour is truly fantastic Aha! Observe the glaze. Mix well. This serves 3-4 people. There isn’t any lump of rice, each grain is separated well. This is the advantage of boiling and cooking the water in excess water instead of cooker. Otherwise it will form lumps, and when you break it, it will be mashed and will turn out like upma or Pongal. So, boiling the rice in water is the easiest way to get such puffy and separated rice grains. That’s it, turn off the gas. Generously add some coriander leaves and mix well. Ready! Just 15-20 minutes to prepare the tomato masala and to mix the rice. If you refrigerate the tomato masala, it will stay fresh for 10 days even though it contains onion and garlic. If you skipped onion and garlic, then it will be fresh for a month. However, increase the oil slightly So that it stays on top. Just mix the tomato masala with rice whenever you want to! Fantastic Tomato rice! Very easy and heavily requested, just for you, In Venkatesh Bhat’s style, only on Idhayam Thotta Samayal, presented by Idhayam.

Hello and welcome to Venkatesh Bhat’s Idhayam Thotta Samayal. Presented by Idhayam oil, Preethi, and Parry’s sugar. Many of you have grown tired of the usual homemade items and are asking for something different. My wish is to help you prepare high quality dishes using ingredients that are already present in your kitchen. Once in a while, we may stray and use exotic ingredients but for me, the thrill lies in creating exciting dishes with common ingredients. So today, using common and simple ingredients, we shall prepare kebabs fried in oil. We will be using golden corn, along with paneer, potato, capsicum, carrot all mixed and dipped into a batter and dusted in cornflakes powder and finally fried. Along with it, we will prepare sweet garlic chilli sauce. Having this kebab alongside that dip, will induce a jolt in you! Wonderful Paneer Corn Kebab. Let’s see how to do it. Firstly, we are going to grind two different ingredients. Here I have 300g of corn. You can get this as frozen/American corn from shops and supermarkets. Transfer it to a mixie jar and grind it 2 times briefly. I’m using Preethi Zodiac Cosmo. It is better if you grind it little less, this has been ground too much! Next, again to the mixie jar, I have normal breakfast cornflakes here. Add 150g to the mixie jar. Grind to a powder. Wow, I didn’t expect it to be this powdery! Good for us. The cornflakes powder is ready. Half the work is done. To the mixing bowl with corn, add 1 medium chopped onion. ½ small chopped capsicum. ½ finely chopped carrot. ¼ handful of cashew nuts. 100g of grated paneer. 100g of grated boiled potatoes. Required salt for Kebab. Little bit of pepper powder. Little bit of Kashmiri Red Chilli powder. Finely chop 2 green chillies and add to the bowl. Add a handful of coriander leaves and mix well till they combine. The ingredients have to bind together. The wetness of the corn will suffice for mixing. Here I have Maida. Spicy Aloo Sandwich:

Ingredients

To Make Spicy Aloo Masala

Oil- 1 Tbsp
Cumin Seeds - 1/2 Tsp
Onion - 2 Nos Chopped
A Piece Of Ginger Chopped
Green Chilli - 3 Nos Chopped
Turmeric Powder - 1/2 Tsp
Chilli Powder - 2 Tsp
Cumin Powder - 1 Tsp
Salt - 1 Tsp
Chaat Masala Powder - 1/2 Tsp
Garam Masala - 1/2 Tsp
Boiled Potato - 5 Nos
Cooked Peas - 1/2 Cup
Chopped Coriander Leaves
Juice Of 1 Lemon

To Make Spicy Aloo Sandwich

Bread
Mint Coriander Chutney
Tomato Ketchup
Cheese Slice
Aloo Masala
Grated Cheese
Butter

Method

For the Aloo Masala

1. Add oil to a pan and roast cumin seeds in it.
2. To this, add onion, ginger, green chilies and saute until the onions turn transparent.
3. Now add turmeric powder, chilli powder, cumin powder, salt, chaat masala powder, garam masala powder and mix everything.
4. Saute this mixture for 1 minute and then add boiled, peeled and roughly cut potatoes.
5. Mix everything once and then mash the potatoes roughly.
6. To the mashed mixture, add cooked green peas, coriander leaves and lemon juice.
7. Give it all a quick mix. Turn off the stove and cool the mixture completely.
8. Aloo masala is ready so keep it aside.

For Spicy Aloo Sandwich

1. Take 2 slices of sandwich bread and on one side of one bread slice, spread some mint coriander chutney and tomato ketchup onto the other slice.
2. On the slice with mint chutney, place a cheese slice.
3. Over it, place the aloo masala and gently spread all across the bread slice.
4. Now, generously grate some cheese on top of aloo masala and close it with the other bread slice which has tomato ketchup on inner side.
5. Gently press the sandwich to secure it.
6. Spread some butter on a sandwich grill and place the prepare raw sandwich on it.
7. Smear some butter on the top most layer of bread and flip it to the bottom to make sure the bread is toasted evenly on both sides.
8. Keep the flame on medium and grill the sandwich on both sides.
9. That's it. Spicy Aloo Sandwich is ready to be served. 
10. Cut it diagonally or half and serve hot with some fries by the side.

Prep Time: 5 mins
Cook Time: 10 mins
Servings: 2

To Make Vegetable Paneer Stir Fry

Oil - 3 Tsp (Buy: https://amzn.to/3KxgtsM)
Garlic - 1 Tbsp
Carrot - 1 Cup
Green Capsicum - 1 Cup
Red Capsicum - 1 Cup
Yellow Capsicum - 1 Cup
Onion - 1 No.
Broccoli - 1 Bowl
Paneer - 200 Gms
Salt - 1 Tsp (Buy: https://amzn.to/3KxgtsM)
Pepper - 1 Tsp (Buy: https://amzn.to/3KxgtsM)
Red Chilli Flakes - 1 Tsp
Soy Sauce - 1 Tsp (Buy: https://amzn.to/3KxgtsM)
Water - 1 Tbsp
Spring Onion Springs


METHOD

1. Take oil in a kadai and heat it.
2. Add chopped garlic and saute for a few seconds.
3. Add carrots, green capsicum, red bell pepper, yellow bell pepper, onions and mix well.
4. Next add, broccoli pieces, mix well and stir fry for about 3 mins.
5. Add paneer pieces and gently mix everything.
6. For seasoning, add salt, pepper powder, red chilli flakes and soya sauce.
7. Mix everything well and add some water. Mix again.
8. Cover the kadai with a lid and cook the veggies and paneer for 5 mins on a low flame.
9. After 5 mins, add chopped spring onions and mix well.
10. Tasty Vegetable Paneer Stir Fry is ready to be served hot and nice.

# Afghani Paneer

 By Hema Subramanian Updated July 24, 2026 

 ![Afghani Paneer](https://homecookingshow.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Afghani-Paneer-1040x884.webp "Afghani Paneer 1") 

If you’re craving something rich, creamy, and absolutely melt-in-your-mouth, Afghani Paneer is about to become your new obsession. It’s one of those dishes that looks luxurious, tastes indulgent, yet is surprisingly simple to make at home.

What makes it special? It blends classic Indian flavors with subtle Afghan influences—think a velvety, cashew-based gravy, gentle spices, and that hint of natural sweetness from slow-cooked onions. 

Every bite is smooth, mild, and perfectly balanced, whether you pair it with soft naan, a warm roti, or a bowl of aromatic basmati rice.

#### A Little History: How Paneer Met Afghanistan

They say paneer, the soft, fresh cheese beloved in Indian cuisine, made its way to the subcontinent with travelers from Afghanistan and Iran centuries ago.

Over time, it became a staple in Indian kitchens, taking on a variety of flavors and styles. Afghani Paneer isn’t an age-old traditional Afghan dish, but rather a beautiful fusion of Mughal-Afghan influences with the creaminess and subtle spice notes that make Indian dishes so comforting.

It’s rich, mildly spiced, and absolutely irresistible—the perfect dish for a special meal or a cozy dinner.

## Breaking Down the Ingredients

Each ingredient plays an essential role in creating the silky, aromatic, and creamy profile of Afghani Paneer:

- Paneer: The star of the dish, soft and creamy paneer cubes soak up all the flavors of the rich gravy. When lightly roasted, they develop a golden crust that adds a delicate bite to the dish.
- Onions & Garlic: These form the base of the gravy. Onions bring a mild sweetness that balances the spice, while garlic adds depth and aroma.
- Ginger & Green Chilies: Ginger gives a warm, earthy kick, while green chilies add just the right amount of heat without overpowering the dish.
- Curd (Yogurt): Acts as a natural tenderizer for the paneer and gives the gravy a creamy, slightly tangy richness.
- Whole Spices (Bay Leaf, Cinnamon, Cardamom, Cloves, Cumin Seeds): These whole spices infuse the oil with fragrance right from the start, ensuring that every bite is layered with warmth and subtle complexity.
- Kashmiri Chili Powder: Adds a beautiful red color and mild heat, making the dish visually appealing without being too spicy.
- Kasuri Methi (Dried Fenugreek Leaves): A game-changer in North Indian dishes, Kasuri methi brings an unmistakable smoky, earthy aroma that enhances the final dish.
- Garam Masala: A blend of warming spices that gives the dish its final boost of flavor.

## Cooking Afghani Paneer: A Step-by-Step Guide

Let’s talk about how to bring this rich, silky paneer dish to life. The process is all about layering flavors, so every step adds depth and richness to the final dish.

First, take your paneer and cut it into generous cubes—not too small, because we want them to stay soft and absorb all that creamy goodness.

Toss the cubes into a simple marinade of salt, pepper, ginger-garlic paste, and a little oil.

Let them sit for about 15 minutes while you move on to the masala. This short resting time helps the paneer soak up all the flavors, making every bite delicious.

Now, let’s build the base of our dish. Heat some oil in a pan and throw in sliced onions, garlic, ginger, and green chilies. Keep stirring and let them turn a nice golden brown—that’s where the magic happens.

The onions soften, release their natural sweetness, and blend beautifully with the warmth of the ginger and garlic. Once everything looks golden and aromatic, transfer this mixture into a blender.

Add a couple of tablespoons of curd, along with Kashmiri chili powder, cumin, coriander powder, and a pinch of salt. Blend everything into a smooth, creamy paste. This is what’s going to give our gravy that luscious, velvety texture without needing cream.

While the masala is blending, heat a little oil in the same pan and toss in the marinated paneer cubes. Let them sizzle until they develop a light golden crust. This gives them a lovely texture—crispy edges with a soft, creamy center. Once done, set them aside.

Now, it’s time to put everything together. In the same pan, add a mix of ghee and oil for that deep, rich flavor. Drop in whole spices—bay leaf, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and cumin seeds. Let them crackle and infuse the oil with their fragrance.

The moment you smell that warm, inviting aroma, pour in the onion-curd masala and let it cook slowly. Keep stirring and watching as the masala thickens and deepens in color. You’ll know it’s ready when you see the oil start to separate from the sides.

Now, bring back the paneer. Gently add the golden cubes to the simmering masala, making sure they’re fully coated in that creamy, spiced sauce. At this point, sprinkle in some garam masala and a little crushed kasuri methi—this is what elevates the dish, adding a final layer of warmth and depth.

Let everything cook together for another 5 minutes, so the paneer absorbs all the flavors.

And that’s it! Serve it hot, maybe with a swirl of fresh cream or a sprinkle of chopped coriander for extra freshness. Scoop it up with soft, buttery naan or pair it with a bowl of steaming jeera rice—either way, this dish is pure comfort on a plate.

### Classic Pairing

Serve it hot with warm naan bread, roti, or paratha. These flatbreads are perfect for scooping up the creamy gravy. Basmati rice is another excellent choice, allowing the rich sauce to coat every grain.

### Garnish

- A sprinkle of freshly chopped cilantro or coriander leaves adds a vibrant touch.
- A drizzle of cream or a few slivered almonds or cashews can elevate the presentation.
- A very small pinch of Garam masala can also be used as a garnish.

### Side Dishes

A simple cucumber raita provides a cooling contrast to the richness of the paneer. A side of lightly spiced vegetable salad can add freshness and balance.

### Airtight Containers

- Use good-quality, leak-proof containers to prevent spills and maintain freshness.
- Separate the paneer and gravy if possible, especially if packing for a longer period. This helps maintain the texture of the paneer.

### Portion Control

- Pack individual portions for convenient reheating.
- Consider using containers with dividers to keep the paneer and rice or bread separate.

### Keeping it Warm

- If possible, use insulated containers to help keep the paneer warm during transport.
- If using plastic containers, allow the food to cool slightly before sealing the container to prevent condensation buildup that can affect texture.

### Reheating

- When reheating, gently warm the paneer in a saucepan over low heat or in the microwave.
- Avoid overheating, as this can cause the paneer to become rubbery.
- If needed, add a splash of milk or cream while reheating to restore the creamy consistency.

# Schezwan Paneer

 By Hema Subramanian Updated August 12, 2026 

 ![Schezwan Paneer](https://homecookingshow.in/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Schezwan-Paneer-1040x884.webp "Schezwan Paneer 1") 

Picture crispy, golden paneer balls—crunchy on the outside, soft and creamy within—tossed in a glossy, fiery-red schezwan sauce that clings to every curve. The sauce is a symphony of flavors: garlicky heat, ginger’s sharp bite, the sweetness of ketchup playing against the salty umami of soy sauce, all punctuated by crunchy capsicum wedges and the fresh bite of spring onions. The aroma is intoxicating—garlic and ginger sizzling in hot oil, that distinctive schezwan chili paste releasing its complex, slightly fermented heat, sesame seeds toasting on top. This dish is bold, unapologetic, and absolutely addictive. It’s the kind of food that makes you reach for one more piece even when you’re full, perfect for weekend dinners, parties, or those evenings when you want restaurant-style Indo-Chinese at home.

Schezwan cuisine, originating from China’s Sichuan province, found its way to India in the mid-20th century and underwent a delicious transformation. Indian Chinese food became its own category—sweeter, spicier, more sauce-heavy than its authentic counterpart, adapted to Indian palates and ingredients. Schezwan paneer is a purely Indian invention, born in the kitchens of Mumbai and Kolkata’s Chinese restaurants where chefs started using paneer—India’s beloved cottage cheese—in place of meat to cater to vegetarian diners. The result? A dish that’s become a staple on Indo-Chinese menus everywhere. I remember the first time I had schezwan paneer at a roadside Chinese stall—the combination of that creamy paneer with the punchy, spicy sauce was a revelation, and I’ve been making versions of it at home ever since.

## The Ingredients

- For the Paneer Balls, you’ll need paneer—grated or crumbled, it forms the soft, protein-rich base. 
- Schezwan sauce adds that signature heat and flavor right into the balls themselves. 
- Salt seasons from within. 
- Fresh coriander leaves bring brightness and herbal notes. 
- Maida (all-purpose flour) and corn flour work together as binders, helping the mixture hold its shape while frying and creating that crispy exterior.
- For the Schezwan Paneer, oil is your cooking medium for that high-heat stir-fry. Garlic is essential—lots of it—for that pungent, aromatic base. 
- Fresh ginger adds warmth and zing. 
- Green chili brings fresh heat that’s different from the schezwan paste’s fermented spice.
- Onion wedges add sweetness and crunch. 
- Green and red capsicum bring color, crunch, and a slight bitterness that balances the sauce. 
- Schezwan chili paste is the soul of this dish—that complex, garlicky, spicy condiment that defines the flavor. 
- Soy sauce adds salty umami depth. 
- Tomato ketchup brings sweetness and helps create that glossy sauce consistency. 
- Salt and pepper season everything. 
- Water loosens the sauce to the right consistency. 
- Spring onion greens add fresh, sharp bite and color. 
- Sesame seeds are the final flourish—nutty, toasted perfection on top.

## How It All Comes Together

Let’s start with prep work because once you start cooking, everything moves fast—that’s the nature of stir-frying. Crumble or grate your paneer until it’s fine and uniform. Finely chop your garlic, ginger, and green chili—these aromatics need to release their flavors quickly in hot oil. Cut your onions and capsicums into chunky wedges, not too small, so they retain some crunch. Make a corn flour slurry by mixing corn flour with a little water until smooth—this will thicken your sauce later. Have a plate ready with some dry corn flour for coating the paneer balls.

Now let’s make those paneer balls. Take your crumbled paneer in a bowl and add schezwan sauce, salt, chopped coriander leaves, maida, and corn flour. Get your hands in there and mix everything really well until it comes together into a smooth, cohesive mixture. The mixture should be moist enough to hold together but not so wet that it falls apart. If it’s too crumbly, add a tiny bit of water. If it’s too wet, add a touch more corn flour.

Rub a little oil on your palms to prevent sticking, then take small portions of the mixture and roll them between your palms into even, golf-ball-sized spheres. Make them all roughly the same size so they cook evenly. Roll each ball in the dry corn flour—this coating is crucial for getting that crispy exterior. Set them aside on a plate.

💡 Pro Tip: Make sure your paneer balls are tightly packed and smooth. Any cracks will cause them to break apart when frying. If a ball cracks while rolling, just squeeze it together and re-roll.

Heat oil in a kadai or deep pan for frying. You want enough oil to submerge the balls at least halfway. Test the temperature by dropping a tiny bit of the mixture in—it should sizzle and rise to the surface immediately. Once the oil is properly hot, gently slide in the paneer balls, working in batches so you don’t overcrowd the pan. Fry them, turning occasionally, until they’re golden brown all over and crispy on the outside. This takes about 3-4 minutes. Remove them with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels. Set them aside while you make the sauce.

In a wide pan or wok—you need space to toss everything together—heat a little oil over high heat. Add your chopped garlic, ginger, and green chili, and sauté for just 30 seconds until they’re fragrant and sizzling. Don’t let the garlic burn or it’ll turn bitter.

Toss in the onion wedges and both capsicums, and stir-fry them on high heat for 2-3 minutes. You want them to soften slightly but still retain their crunch—that texture contrast is important. Keep everything moving in the pan so nothing burns.

Now add your schezwan chili paste, soy sauce, tomato ketchup, salt, and pepper. Mix everything together really well so the vegetables get coated in that sauce. Add a splash of water to loosen things up and let it all cook together for a minute or two, allowing those flavors to meld.

💡 Pro Tip: If you like your sauce extra spicy, add an extra teaspoon of schezwan paste. If you want it milder and sweeter, add a bit more ketchup. This is your chance to customize the heat level.

Pour in your corn flour slurry and mix quickly. The sauce will start to thicken and turn glossy within seconds. Keep stirring so it doesn’t form lumps. You want a sauce that’s thick enough to coat the back of a spoon but still flows easily.

Add your chopped spring onion greens and toss everything together. Now gently add those fried paneer balls and fold them into the sauce, coating each one thoroughly without breaking them apart. Work quickly but gently—you want every ball glistening with that red sauce.

Sprinkle sesame seeds over the top for that final touch of nutty flavor and visual appeal. Give it one last gentle toss and you’re done.

## What Goes Along

Schezwan paneer is rich and saucy, so it pairs beautifully with plain steamed rice or egg fried rice to soak up all that delicious sauce. Hakka noodles make it a complete Indo-Chinese feast. Some people love it with butter garlic naan or plain naan. A side of vegetable manchurian or spring rolls turns this into a full-blown Chinese spread. A simple cucumber and carrot salad with a light vinegar dressing cuts through the richness nicely.

I love it with:

- Chili Garlic Noodles
- Veg Malaysian Fried Rice (Nasi Goreng Kampung)
- Egg Fried Rice

## How to Serve

Serve this hot—and I mean straight off the stove if possible. The paneer balls should still be crispy on the outside, and the sauce should be steaming. Pile it high on a serving platter, garnish with extra spring onions and sesame seeds if you’re feeling fancy, and watch it disappear. This is sharing food—put it in the center of the table with serving spoons and let everyone dig in.

## How to Store

Store the schezwan paneer in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days. The paneer balls will soften in the sauce, so they won’t be crispy anymore, but they’ll still taste delicious. Don’t store the fried paneer balls separately in the sauce for more than a few hours before serving, or they’ll get soggy.

## How to Reheat

Reheat gently in a pan over medium heat, adding a splash of water if the sauce has thickened too much. You can also microwave it for 1-2 minutes, stirring halfway through. If you want to bring back some crispiness to the paneer balls, you can re-fry them quickly before adding them to the reheated sauce, though this is extra effort most people skip.

## Common Substitutions

Out of schezwan paste? Make your own with dried red chilies, garlic, ginger, vinegar, and soy sauce blended together, or substitute with red chili sauce mixed with garlic paste (it won’t be quite the same but works in a pinch). 

Can’t find spring onions? Regular onion greens or even the green parts of leeks work. 

No capsicum? Use any crunchy vegetables like baby corn, carrots, or snow peas. 

If you want to make this gluten-free, use rice flour instead of maida and check that your soy sauce is gluten-free (tamari works great).

🌿 Vegan Swap: Replace paneer with firm tofu—press it well to remove excess moisture, then crumble and proceed exactly as written. Everything else in this recipe is already plant-based, so it’s an easy swap that works beautifully.

## Packing for a Party / Bulk Preparation

This dish is a party superstar. You can make the paneer balls a few hours ahead and keep them at room temperature, then fry them just before your guests arrive. The sauce comes together in minutes, so you can cook it fresh when serving. For a crowd, double or triple the recipe—just fry the paneer balls in batches and make the sauce in a larger wok. If you’re meal prepping, you can prepare the paneer mixture and shape the balls, then freeze them unfried. Fry them straight from frozen when you’re ready to cook—they’ll just take a minute or two longer. The schezwan sauce also freezes well, so make a big batch and portion it out for quick weeknight dinners.

### My paneer balls keep breaking while frying. What should I do? 

This usually happens if the mixture is too dry. Add a little more corn flour or maida to bind it properly. Also, make sure the oil is hot before frying.

### Can I bake or air-fry the paneer balls instead of deep-frying? 

Yes! Bake at 180°C (350°F) for about 15-20 minutes, flipping halfway. For air-frying, cook at 180°C for around 10-12 minutes

### Why do we coat the paneer balls in corn flour before frying? 

The corn flour coating helps create a crispy outer layer and prevents the balls from absorbing too much oil.

### Can I skip the corn flour coating? 

You can, but the texture will be slightly different. The coating gives a nice crunch.

### How do I know when the oil is ready for frying? 

Drop a tiny piece of the mixture into the oil—if it sizzles and floats up immediately, the oil is ready.

### Can I adjust the spice level of the sauce? 

Absolutely! Reduce the schezwan sauce and green chilli if you prefer a milder taste, or add extra chilli flakes for more heat.

### My sauce is too thick. How do I fix it? 

Add a little water and mix well until you get the desired consistency.

### Should I add the paneer balls immediately after making the sauce? 

It’s best to add them just before serving so they stay crispy. Letting them sit in the sauce too long can make them soft.

### Can I make this dish ahead of time? 

Yes! You can prepare the paneer balls and sauce separately. Just reheat the sauce and toss in the paneer balls before serving.

### Why do we sprinkle sesame seeds at the end? 

Sesame seeds add a slight crunch and enhance the overall flavor of the dish.

### What can I serve with Schezwan Paneer? 

It pairs well with fried rice, noodles, or even as a side with roti or naan.

### Is Schezwan Paneer very spicy? 

It can be. Adjust heat by reducing Schezwan sauce and green chilli. You can also add a splash of tomato ketchup to balance it.

### What is the best paneer texture for this recipe? 

Firm but fresh paneer works best. Too soft paneer won’t hold shape well for the paneer balls.

### What can I serve Schezwan Paneer with? 

Serve with fried rice, noodles, or as a standalone starter with extra Schezwan dip.

To Make Kaju Paneer Curry

Cashew Nuts - 25 Nos
Capsicum - 1 No.
Paneer - 400 Gms
Ghee - 2 Tbsp
Oil - 3 Tbsp
Whole Spices 
( Cinnamon, Cloves, Cardamom, Bay Leaf,  
  Peppercorns, Shahi Jeera, Cumin Seeds, Fennel Seeds )
Onion - 3 Nos

Tomato Puree

Method:
1. Add ghee to a pan and roast a few cashewnuts in it until they are golden brown in colour.Keep them aside.
2. To the same pan, add capsicum wedges and slightly toast. Keep them aside.
3. Add ghee again to the same and add evenly cut paneer cubes. Roast until they are golden brown in colour on all sides. It takes about 5-7 minutes to roast the paneer. Keep them aside.
4. Soak 25 cashewnuts in water for at least one hour and then grind them into a fine paste. Keep it aside.
5. Take ghee in a wide kadai. Add oil to it.
6. Add the whole spices, saute for a few seconds and then add in the chopped onions along with slit green chillies.
7. Saute the onions for a minimum of 10-15 minutes for them to brown.
8. Then add in ginger garlic paste and mix.
9. Add in the tomato puree and cook until the oil separates.
10. Then add salt, turmeric powder, red chilli powder, coriander powder, cumin powder, sugar and mix it all well.
11. Add in cashewnut paste, mix and add water to dilute the masala.
12. Cook the gravy for 5-10 seconds and add the roasted capsicum, cashewnuts and fried paneer. Mix everything well.
13. Cover the kadai with a lid and cook the curry for about 5 mins.
14. After 5 mins, add in garam masala, crushed kasuri methi and mix.
15. Finally garnish the curry with some chopped coriander leaves.
16. Rich and flavorful Kaju Paneer Curry is ready to be served hot with any Indian bread of your choice.

To make Malai Paneer:

2. Add a little water to the mixer jar and remove the remaining paste sticking in it.

Ginger Garlic Paste - 1 1/2 Tsp
Tomato - 5 Nos
Turmeric Powder - 1/4 Tsp
Salt - 1 Tsp
Red Chilli Powder - 3 Tsp
Coriander Powder - 1 Tsp
Cumin Powder - 1 Tsp
Gram Flour - 2 Tsp
Salt - 1/2 Tsp
Sugar - 1/2 Tsp
Kasuri Methi
Water 

Method:

1. Take a kadai and heat ghee with oil.
2. Add the whole spices, cumin seeds and bay leaf.
3. After a few seconds, add the chopped onions and fry until they are golden brown in colour.
4. Add ginger garlic paste and saute.
5. To this, add grated tomatoes and cook for 5 mins to make sure the raw smell goes away.
6. Now add turmeric powder, salt, chili powder, cumin powder and coriander powder.
7. Mix well and cook until oil in the gravy is separated.
8. After the oil begins to separate, add besan and mix again.
9. After a min, add 2 cups of water cook the gravy on medium flame for 10 mins.
10. Once again when the oil begins to separate, add salt, sugar and mix well.
11. Add the paneer which has been cut into large cubes.
12. Now add garam masala. Mix and simmer for about 5 mins.
13. Turn off the stove. Crush a little kasuri methi and add it to the curry
14. Transfer the curry into another plate and garnish it with chopped coriander.
15. Yummy Dhaba style Paneer Masala is ready to be served hot.
